prompt: What mostly separates one file format from another, as far as speed goes?
hint: Think of the disk, not the syntax.

choices.text: The punctuation it uses to separate values, commas or braces
choices.why: Spelling is the visible difference and the least important one.

choices.text: Which values sit next to each other on the disk, and so what a reader must pass over
choices.why: Right: the layout decides what a reader has to pass over.

choices.text: The file extension, which tells the operating system how to open it
choices.why: An extension is a label; renaming a file changes nothing inside it.

choices.text: Whether the format was published as an open standard
choices.why: All five here are open; that says nothing about layout.

prompt: The app writes one ride the moment a bicycle is docked. Which layout makes that write cheap?
hint: Where does the new ride go in each layout?

choices.text: Column-oriented, because each value lands in the run for its own column
choices.why: That is seven places to write for one ride.

choices.text: Either, because a write costs the same in any layout
choices.why: The table in the section shows the two differ exactly here.

choices.text: Row-oriented, where the whole ride is one write at the end
choices.why: Right: one write at the end of the file.

choices.text: Column-oriented, once the values are compressed
choices.why: Compression makes the file smaller, not the single append cheaper.

prompt: Why does a column of `start_station` values compress so well in a columnar file?
hint: Look at the second half of the run of `rides.py`.

choices.text: Station codes are short strings
choices.why: Short helps a little; repetition is what helps a lot.

choices.text: Its neighbours repeat twelve values
choices.why: Right: alike values side by side are what a compressor feeds on.

choices.text: Columnar files sort every column alphabetically
choices.why: Nothing is sorted; the rows keep the order they were written in.

choices.text: The column is stored apart from the timestamps
choices.why: Being apart matters only because what is left together is alike.

prompt: Match each format to its layout.
hint: Two of the five store columns.

pairs.right: rows, as text with one header
rows, as text with names on each

prompt: In the run of `comma.py`, how many fields did splitting on commas find in the line of ride R000101?
hint: Its note has a comma inside.

prompt: How does RFC 4180 write a field that contains a comma?
hint: Look at `notes.csv`.

choices.text: It escapes the comma with a backslash before it
choices.why: That is a habit from other formats; RFC 4180 has no backslash rule.

choices.text: It replaces the comma with a semicolon in that field
choices.why: That would change the data; the comma survives as it is.

choices.text: It wraps the whole field in a pair of double quotes
choices.why: Right, and a quote inside such a field is written twice.

choices.text: It is not allowed; such a field must be cleaned first
choices.why: It is allowed, and the `csv` module wrote one.

prompt: A program reads `minutes` from a CSV and adds 5 to it, and Python raises `TypeError`. Why?
hint: What did `repr(rows[1][2])` print?

choices.text: The value came back as the string `'12'`, and adding an int to a string raises it
choices.why: Right: CSV carries text, and the reader has to convert it.

choices.text: The `csv` module stores numbers as floats, which cannot be added to integers
choices.why: A float and an int add perfectly well; and nothing was a float.

choices.text: The file was written with the wrong encoding
choices.why: An encoding problem garbles letters; it does not change a type.

choices.text: The column was quoted, which marks it as text
choices.why: `12` was not quoted, and quotes in CSV are about commas, not types.

prompt: A reader opens a UTF-8 export as Latin-1. What happens to "Praça Tiradentes"?
hint: The run showed it.

choices.text: Python raises a `UnicodeDecodeError` and stops
choices.why: Latin-1 can decode any byte, so nothing stops: that is the danger.

choices.text: The `ç` is dropped and the rest reads fine
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; one character becomes two.

choices.text: It becomes `PraÃ§a`, with no error
choices.why: Right: two bytes read as two characters, silently.

choices.text: The line is split in two at the cedilla
choices.why: The cedilla is not a line break in either encoding.

prompt: Which of these has no type of its own in JSON?
hint: Count the six.

choices.text: A missing value, written as `null`
choices.why: `null` is one of the six.

choices.text: A date, which has to be spelt as a string or a number
choices.why: Right: it has to be spelt as a string or a number.

choices.text: A list of values, written between brackets
choices.why: An array is one of the six.

choices.text: A true-or-false value
choices.why: `true` and `false` are one of the six.

prompt: Of the 162 bytes of the ride printed by `as_json.py`, how many were field names in quotes?
hint: The last line of the run.

prompt: A nightly job writes a file of 2 million events. Why would you choose JSON Lines over one JSON array?
hint: Think about a reader, and about a file cut off halfway.

choices.text: JSON Lines carries more types than an array of the same objects
choices.why: Both use the same six types.

choices.text: A JSON array cannot hold more than a million elements
choices.why: There is no such limit in JSON.

choices.text: JSON Lines drops the field names, so the file is smaller
choices.why: Every line still carries every name.

choices.text: It is read one line at a time, and splits at any line break
choices.why: Right, and a damaged line costs one record, not the file.

prompt: In JSON Lines, every record sits on its own ___.
hint: The name says it.

prompt: Put in order what a Parquet reader does to average `minutes` for rides after 25 September.
hint: It starts at the end of the file.
items: read the last bytes to learn the footer’s length
rule out row groups whose statistics end too early
read the needed column chunks of the groups left
trap: Nothing about the rows is known before the footer has been read.

prompt: Into how many row groups did `as_parquet.py` cut the 50,000 rides?
hint: Groups of 20,000.

prompt: How did `as_parquet.py` know the first and last time in each row group without reading any ride?
hint: `metadata` is one part of the file.

choices.text: From the min and max of `started_at` that the footer keeps for each row group
choices.why: Right: statistics per column chunk, kept in the footer.

choices.text: It worked them out from the row-group size and the seed in `rides.py`
choices.why: It never looked at `rides.py`; it read the file it wrote.

choices.text: Parquet sorts each group, so the first and last rows give the answer
choices.why: Parquet sorts nothing, and reading those rows would be reading rides.

choices.text: pyarrow scans the `started_at` pages, which are small
choices.why: Scanning pages is reading rides; it read the footer only.

prompt: Davi writes the month of rides to Parquet sorted by `bike_id` instead of by time. What happens to a question about rides after 25 September?
hint: What would each group’s min and max of `started_at` be?

choices.text: It fails, because the statistics no longer match the data
choices.why: The statistics are still true; they just stop being useful.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because pyarrow re-sorts by time when it writes
choices.why: The writer keeps the order it is given.

choices.text: Hardly any row group is skipped, because each spans the month
choices.why: Right: each group spans the whole month, so none can be ruled out by date.

choices.text: It is answered from the footer without reading any column
choices.why: The footer rules groups out; it does not hold the minutes to average.

prompt: `start_station` took 10,170 bytes encoded and compressed, and 160,049 with neither. What did most of the work?
hint: Twelve values, 20,000 rows.

choices.text: Snappy compression, which shrinks any text by about this much
choices.why: The dictionary had already shrunk it; Snappy found little left.

choices.text: The dictionary: twelve codes stored once, a small number per row
choices.why: Right: Snappy then had little left to do.

choices.text: The footer statistics, which replace repeated values with a min and a max
choices.why: Statistics describe a chunk; they do not replace its values.

choices.text: Removing the four-byte lengths in front of each code
choices.why: That alone would halve it, not divide it by fifteen.

prompt: Skipping row groups by reading their statistics is called predicate ___.
hint: The filter is pushed down to the file.

prompt: Where does an Avro file keep the names of its fields?
hint: Look at the first hundred bytes.

choices.text: Before each value, as in JSON
choices.why: Avro records carry no names; that is why they are small.

choices.text: In a separate `.avsc` file that has to travel with it
choices.why: A schema can be kept in such a file, but the container carries its own.

choices.text: In the footer, after the last block
choices.why: That is Parquet’s and ORC’s place; Avro’s is the other end.

choices.text: In the header, as JSON
choices.why: Right: the schema as JSON, under `avro.schema`.

prompt: A ride written at 06:01:23 in Curitiba came back from the Avro file as 09:01:23+00:00. What does that mean?
hint: `timestamp-millis` holds one number.

choices.text: The same instant, printed in UTC, because the value holds no time zone of its own
choices.why: Right: milliseconds since 1970 in UTC, and nothing else.

choices.text: fastavro added three hours by mistake, which is a bug in the library
choices.why: 06:01 at UTC−3 and 09:01 at UTC are the same moment.

choices.text: The ride is now recorded as starting three hours later
choices.why: The instant did not move; only how it is printed did.

choices.text: Avro cannot store times, so it stored the text of the time in UTC
choices.why: It stored a number, through a logical type.

prompt: Why does every Avro block end with the same sync marker?
hint: Imagine starting to read in the middle of a large file.

choices.text: To check that no block was written twice
choices.why: A repeated block would carry the same marker too.

choices.text: So a reader finds where a block starts
choices.why: Right: which is what makes the file splittable.

choices.text: To separate the field values inside each record
choices.why: Records have no separators; the schema says where each value ends.

choices.text: To mark where the compression codec changes in the file
choices.why: One codec is named in the header for the whole file.

prompt: Which of these make Avro a good fit for messages on a stream? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of one event, sent alone.

choices.text: A record is small, with no names in it
choices.why: Yes: a few dozen bytes for a ride.

choices.text: It is row-oriented, so one record is written whole
choices.why: Yes: one event, one write.

choices.text: Old data can be read with a new schema, by rules
choices.why: Yes: readers and writers change at different times.

choices.text: A reader can fetch one column without the others
choices.why: No: that is the columnar formats’ strength, not Avro’s.

prompt: `as_orc.py` asked for stripes of 64 KiB and got 33,792 rows and 16,208 rows. Why are they not round numbers?
hint: What was the limit expressed in?

choices.text: A stripe is cut when it reaches a size, not a row count
choices.why: Right: the writer closes a stripe when its estimate reaches the limit.

choices.text: ORC drops rows that do not fit evenly into a stripe
choices.why: Both stripes add up to 50,000; nothing was dropped.

choices.text: zstd compression removed the duplicated rides first
choices.why: There were no duplicates, and compression removes no rows.

choices.text: The row index needs a multiple of 10,000 and rounds the rest
choices.why: Neither number is a multiple of 10,000, and nothing was rounded.

prompt: A team runs a large Hive installation whose tables take updates and deletes. Which format do those tables need?
hint: Hive’s transactional tables.

choices.text: Parquet, because it is the default of most new platforms
choices.why: Most new platforms are not this one; Hive’s transactional tables say otherwise.

choices.text: Avro, because a format for updates has to be row-oriented
choices.why: Hive’s transactional tables are columnar; layout is not the deciding fact here.

choices.text: ORC, because Hive’s transactional mode accepts nothing else
choices.why: Right: Hive’s transactional tables require it.

choices.text: Any of the three binary formats, chosen per table
choices.why: Transactional tables in Hive accept one format.

prompt: Why did `five.py` pass `compression="none"` to the Parquet writer only?
hint: What do the other writers do by default?

choices.text: Parquet cannot be read back by pyarrow when it is compressed
choices.why: `as_parquet.py` read back a Snappy file without trouble.

choices.text: Of the five, only its writer compresses when nobody asks
choices.why: Right: so all five are compared on layout alone.

choices.text: To make Parquet look smaller than ORC in the comparison
choices.why: It came out larger than ORC; the aim was a fair comparison.

choices.text: The other four formats have no compression to switch off

prompt: Why does this lesson compare bytes rather than seconds?
hint: Which of the two would be the same on your machine?

choices.text: Seconds are too small to measure on 50,000 rows
choices.why: They are measurable; they are just not repeatable elsewhere.

choices.text: Reading time does not depend on the format
choices.why: It does; bytes read are a large part of it.

choices.text: Bytes are the same on every machine
choices.why: Right, and they are what disks read and bills charge.

choices.text: pyarrow does not report how long a read took
choices.why: Any program can time itself; the problem is what the number means elsewhere.

prompt: The gzipped CSV, 570,459 bytes, was smaller than every Parquet file. Why is it still the worse choice for analysis?
hint: Size is one of four things.

choices.text: gzip loses data that Parquet’s codecs keep
choices.why: gzip is lossless; the CSV comes back byte for byte.

choices.text: It must be read whole, from the start
choices.why: Right: no columns to skip to, and no place to split it.

choices.text: Spreadsheets cannot open a gzipped file
choices.why: Analysis here is done by programs, and that is not the reason.

choices.text: A gzipped file is larger again once it is in memory
choices.why: So is Parquet; every compressed file grows when decompressed.

prompt: Why can ten workers share one large Parquet file but not one large `.csv.gz`?
hint: Where can each one start?

choices.text: Parquet files are smaller, so each worker is given less to read
choices.why: Here the gzipped CSV was smaller; size is not what splits.

choices.text: Parquet compresses each page apart, and the footer says where
choices.why: Right: a worker can start at any row group.

choices.text: gzip uses a password that only one process at a time can hold
choices.why: gzip has no password; the stream has to be read from its start.

choices.text: A CSV has no header to tell workers the column names
choices.why: This one has a header; the problem is the gzip stream.

prompt: In `squeeze.py`, which codec shrank the Parquet file least?

choices.text: gzip, the oldest of the three
choices.why: It took the file to 638,037, about half.

choices.text: zstd, which was released by Facebook
choices.why: It was the smallest Parquet, 633,691.

choices.text: Snappy
choices.why: Right: 907,079 bytes, the trade for speed.

choices.text: They all came out within a few bytes
choices.why: Snappy was 270,000 bytes behind the other two.

prompt: Which of these files can be split between workers without reading them from the start? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look for markers, footers or a codec that splits.

choices.text: An Avro file compressed with a codec
choices.why: Yes: each block is compressed alone and ends with the sync marker.

choices.text: A Parquet file compressed with zstd
choices.why: Yes: pages are compressed inside row groups the footer locates.

choices.text: A CSV compressed with gzip
choices.why: No: one stream, from the first byte.

choices.text: A JSON Lines file compressed with gzip
choices.why: No: the lines are splittable, the gzip stream around them is not.
